title: Gadget Organizer Ideas: How to Sort Chargers, Cables, Power Banks and Small Devices at Home and on the Road
seoTitle: Gadget Organizer Ideas for Cables and Chargers
excerpt: Gadget organizer ideas: set up a daily charging spot, divide a drawer for spare cables, box tiny parts, pack a travel pouch and follow FAA rules for power banks and spare batteries.
imageCaption: A hot pink set of three packing cubes and three pouches with three frosted storage bags. Photo: Sesoris product catalog.
content: A good **gadget organizer** gives every charger, cable, power bank and small device a fixed spot, both at home and in your bag. At home, sort gadgets into a drop zone by the door, a charging station, a drawer for spares and a box for rarely used items. For travel, pack cables and chargers in a see-through pouch, keep spare lithium batteries and power banks in your carry-on, and protect their terminals from short circuit. Label cords, coil them loosely and clear out what you no longer use.

Gadgets multiply quietly. A new phone arrives with a new cable, the old charger stays in a drawer, earbuds come with their own case, and suddenly there is a tangle of cords that nobody can identify. This guide shows how to organize gadgets and their accessories around the way you actually use them, with ideas for home, the desk and travel, plus the safety rules that matter for batteries.
## What Counts as a Gadget, and Why They Get Messy
For organizing purposes, gadgets fall into four groups:

- **Devices:** phones, tablets, e-readers, earbuds, smartwatches, cameras and handheld game consoles.
- **Power:** chargers, wall plugs, power banks and spare batteries.
- **Cables and adapters:** charging cables, video cables, card readers and plug adapters.
- **Small accessories:** memory cards, SIM tools, styluses, lens cloths and spare ear tips.

They get messy for three reasons. They are small, so they slip into whatever space is nearby. They come with accessories that look alike, so nobody can tell which cable fits which device. And they move around all day, from bedroom to kitchen to bag, so they rarely end up in the same place twice. A gadget organizer solves all three by giving each group a home and a label.
## Gadget Organizer Options at a Glance

| Organizer type | Best for | Where it works | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Zippered pouch or travel case | Cables, chargers, earbuds on the go | Backpacks, carry-ons, work bags | Overstuffing, which bends cables |
| Drawer trays | Spare cables, adapters, small accessories | Desk or kitchen drawers | Trays that are too deep to see into |
| Small clear boxes with lids | Memory cards, SIM tools, tiny parts | Drawers and shelves | Losing track without labels |
| Wall or door pocket organizer | Daily chargers, keys, glasses | Entryways, bedrooms | Pockets that are too small for plugs |
| Charging station spot | Phones, watches, earbuds overnight | Kitchen counter, hallway table | Too many cords in one place |
You do not need every type. Most homes need one daily charging spot, one drawer for spares and one travel pouch.
## Step 1: Gather Every Gadget and Cable in One Place
Start by collecting every device, charger, cable and accessory from around the house. Check drawers, bags, the car, nightstands and the back of the TV unit. Put everything on a table.
Then sort:

1. **Match each cable and charger to a device.** Plug it in if you are not sure.
2. **Set aside duplicates.** Decide how many of each cable type you really need.
3. **Pull out anything broken or frayed.** Damaged cables and chargers should not go back into use.
4. **Separate old devices** you no longer use for donation, resale or recycling.

If you are clearing out old devices or batteries, do not throw them in the trash. The EPA says lithium-ion batteries and devices containing them should not go in household garbage or recycling bins, and should be taken to separate recycling or household hazardous waste collection points. To prevent fires, it advises taping battery terminals or placing batteries in separate plastic bags ([EPA](https://www.epa.gov/recycle/used-lithium-ion-batteries)).
Our guide on [how to organize a junk drawer](/blog/how-to-organize-a-junk-drawer-step-by-step-tutorial-2026) uses the same sort-first method for all the small things that end up in one drawer.
## Step 2: Create a Daily Charging Spot
The gadgets you use every day need a home that is quick to reach. A charging spot stops phones and earbuds from ending up on random counters with cables strung across the room.

- **Choose one location** near an outlet, such as a hallway table, a kitchen corner or a shelf by the door.
- **Limit it to daily devices.** Phones, watches, earbuds and maybe a tablet.
- **Use one cable per device** and leave the cables plugged in, so charging is a one-step habit.
- **Keep it tidy.** Cable clips or a small tray keep cords from sliding behind furniture.

## Step 3: Organize a Drawer for Spare Cables and Accessories
Spare cables, adapters and accessories do not need to be on display, but they should be easy to find. A single drawer, divided into sections, works well.

- **Divide by type:** charging cables, video cables, adapters, wall plugs and small parts.
- **Coil cables loosely** and secure them with a reusable tie or a rubber band. Tight wrapping can stress the cable near the plug.
- **Label each cable** with tape or a tag showing which device it fits.
- **Keep the most-used items at the front.**

## Step 4: Use Small Boxes for Tiny Parts
Memory cards, SIM tools, spare ear tips and tiny adapters are the easiest items to lose. Small boxes with snap lids keep them together.

Use the square boxes for memory cards and SIM tools, and the rectangular ones for spare ear tips, short cables and adapters. Label the lid, because clear plastic shows what is inside but not which device it belongs to.
## Step 5: Build a Travel Gadget Pouch
A dedicated travel pouch saves you from packing cables from scratch every trip. Keep it stocked and ready.
**What to put in a travel gadget pouch:**

- One charging cable for each device you travel with
- A wall charger, ideally one with more than one port
- A power bank, if you use one
- Earbuds and their case
- A plug adapter if you travel internationally
- A small box for memory cards or a SIM tool

## Travel Rules for Power Banks and Spare Batteries

Batteries are the one part of gadget organizing where rules really matter. According to the FAA, spare lithium batteries, including power banks and cell phone battery charging cases, must be carried in carry-on baggage only. If a carry-on bag is checked at the gate or planeside, spare lithium batteries and power banks must be removed and kept with the passenger in the cabin ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/lithium-batteries)).

The FAA also requires battery terminals to be protected from short circuit, meaning the terminals must not touch other metal. Methods it lists include leaving batteries in their retail packaging, covering terminals with tape, using a battery case or sleeve, or putting them snugly in a plastic bag or protective pouch ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/lithium-batteries)).

On size, the FAA limits lithium ion batteries to 100 watt hours per battery, and with airline approval passengers may carry up to two spare larger lithium ion batteries of 101 to 160 watt hours ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/lithium-batteries)). The TSA states that power banks containing a lithium ion battery must be packed in carry-on bags and are not allowed in checked bags ([TSA](https://www.tsa.gov/travel/security-screening/whatcanibring/items/power-banks)).
For your gadget organizer, that means:

- **Keep the power bank pouch in your personal item or carry-on**, never in a suitcase you might check.
- **Give each spare battery its own sleeve or bag**, or tape the terminals.
- **Do not mix loose batteries with coins, keys or metal clips** in the same pocket.
- **Check the watt-hour rating** printed on large power banks before you fly.
Airlines can have their own rules, so check with your carrier before a trip.
## Keep Travel Documents and Your Phone Together
On travel days, your phone, passport and boarding pass are the gadgets and papers you reach for most. Keeping them in one case saves digging through bags at security and the gate.

## Organize Gadgets at Your Desk
A desk often becomes the main gadget hub, with a laptop, monitor, phone, headphones and their cables all in one place.

- **Route cables behind or under the desk** with clips or a cable tray.
- **Keep one charging cable on the desk** for your phone and store spares in a drawer.
- **Give headphones a hook or stand** so they do not sit on papers.
- **Store rarely used cables**, such as old video adapters, in a labeled box rather than on the desk.
Our [desk cable management ideas](/blog/desk-cable-management-ideas) and [cable management guide](/blog/cable-management) cover clips, trays and under-desk routing in detail.
## Organize Gadgets in the Bedroom
Bedside tables collect phones, e-readers, watches and earbuds every night.

- **Keep one charging cable per device** at the bedside and nothing more.
- **Use a small tray** to hold earbuds and a watch so they do not fall behind the nightstand.
- **Store spare cables elsewhere** so the nightstand drawer does not become a second junk drawer.
Our [nightstand organization ideas](/blog/nightstand-organization-ideas) have more ways to keep a bedside table clear.
## Organize Shared and Family Gadgets
In a family home, tablets, game controllers and headphones are often shared, which makes them the most likely to go missing.

- **Give shared devices one home**, such as a basket or shelf in the living room, and make returning them part of the evening reset.
- **Charge shared devices in a common spot** rather than in bedrooms, so everyone knows where to find them.
- **Use one color of label per person** for personal cables and earbuds, so mix-ups end quickly.
- **Keep game controllers and their cables together** in one bin near the console.
- **Store kids' headphones and tablets at a height they can reach**, so they can put them away without help.
A simple rule helps: if a device leaves its home, it goes back before bed. Over a few weeks, that one habit does more than any organizer.
## Label Everything
Labels are what turn a box of cables into a system.

- **Cable labels:** a small piece of tape or a tag near the plug with the device name.
- **Box labels:** on the lid and the front, so you can read them from above or the side.
- **Drawer labels:** on the drawer front or the edge of each tray.
- **Color coding:** one color per family member or per device type, if that helps.
## Maintenance: A Quick Gadget Reset
Gadget clutter comes back quickly, so build a short reset into your routine.

- **Weekly:** return cables and devices to their homes, and recharge the power bank.
- **Monthly:** check the travel pouch is complete and remove anything that crept in.
- **Twice a year:** sort the spare cable drawer, recycle what you no longer need and check for damaged cables.

When you buy a new device, decide where its cable and charger will live before you open the box. Our [travel gear guide](/blog/travel-gear) is useful when you are deciding which gadgets are worth taking on trips.
## Common Gadget Organizing Mistakes

- **Keeping every cable that ever came in a box.**
- **Wrapping cables tightly around chargers**, which can strain the cable near the plug.
- **Mixing loose batteries with metal items** in a pocket or drawer.
- **Packing power banks in checked luggage.**
- **Skipping labels**, so nobody knows which cable fits which device.
- **Using organizers that are too small** for plugs and chargers.
## Frequently Asked Questions
**Q: What is a gadget organizer?**
It is any pouch, tray, box or wall pocket that gives chargers, cables, power banks and small devices a fixed place, so they do not end up tangled or lost.
**Q: How do I organize chargers and cables at home?**
Gather them in one place, match each cable to a device, recycle broken ones, label what you keep, and store spares in a divided drawer with daily cables at a single charging spot.
**Q: Can I pack a power bank in checked luggage?**
No. The FAA and TSA say spare lithium batteries, including power banks, must be carried in carry-on baggage only.
**Q: How do I protect spare batteries when traveling?**
The FAA says terminals must be protected from short circuit, for example by leaving batteries in retail packaging, taping the terminals, or using a battery case, sleeve or snug plastic bag.
**Q: What should go in a travel gadget pouch?**
A charging cable for each device, a wall charger, earbuds, a power bank, a plug adapter for international trips and a small box for memory cards or a SIM tool.
**Q: How do I dispose of old gadgets and batteries?**

The EPA says lithium-ion batteries and devices containing them should not go in household trash or recycling bins and should be taken to separate recycling or household hazardous waste collection points.
**Q: How should I coil cables so they last?**
Coil them loosely and secure them with a reusable tie or rubber band, rather than wrapping them tightly around a charger.
**Q: Where should I keep everyday chargers?**
At one charging spot near an outlet, such as a hallway table, kitchen corner or bedside, with one cable per daily device.
## Final Thoughts

A gadget organizer works when every device and cable has one home. Sort and label what you own, recycle what you do not need, set up a daily charging spot, divide a drawer for spares and keep a travel pouch stocked. Follow the battery rules when you fly, and give the system a quick reset every week so cables never get the chance to tangle again.
